Enthuse means to express great excitement about something, or to make someone else feel great excitement. Those are its two jobs as a verb, and everything else flows from these two uses.
Use 1 — To Express Enthusiasm (The Most Common Use)

When a person enthuses, they talk about or react to something with obvious, energetic excitement. Not mild interest. Not a polite smile. Real, bubbling-over enthusiasm that others can clearly see and hear.

Think of it as enthusiasm in action — visible, outward, and hard to miss.

Examples:

  • "She enthused about her new job for the entire dinner."

Here, she didn't just mention her job. She talked about it with glowing, lively excitement — probably at length, with lots of energy.

  • "He enthused over every dish the chef brought to the table."

He reacted to each dish with visible delight and enthusiasm.

  • "The journalist enthused about the film in her review."

She praised it with obvious personal excitement, not dry professionalism.

The prepositions you use with this sense: about and over are the most natural ones.

  • enthuse about something
  • enthuse over something
Use 2 — To Fill Someone Else With Enthusiasm

When something enthuses a person, it causes that person to feel excited, motivated, and eager. Here, the verb is transitive — it takes a direct object (a person or group being enthused).

Examples:

  • "The coach's speech enthused the entire team."

The speech didn't just inform the players — it filled them with genuine excitement and fighting spirit.

  • "The documentary enthused a whole new generation of young scientists."

It sparked real enthusiasm in them, possibly inspiring career choices or new passions.

  • "Nothing about the project enthused her."

Nothing about it sparked any excitement in her at all.

You will very often see enthused used as a descriptive word (adjective), meaning feeling enthusiastic or filled with enthusiasm. It comes directly from this verb.

  • "She was enthused by the idea." → She felt genuinely excited about it.
  • "He didn't seem very enthused about the plan." → He showed little or no enthusiasm for it.
  • "The audience left the hall feeling enthused and inspired."

This passive/adjectival form is extremely common in everyday speech, so it's worth recognising it as a natural extension of the verb.

Whether someone is enthusing about something or someone/something is enthusing a person — the emotion involved is always strong, genuine, and outwardly visible excitement. It's not quiet contentment. It's not reluctant approval. It's the kind of positive energy that tends to light up a person's voice, gestures, and words.

This means "enthuse" carries a slightly warmer, more expressive quality than simple words like "like" or "enjoy." When you say someone enthused about something, you're painting a picture of them practically glowing with excitement.
When and Where People Use This Word

Enthuse is slightly informal. It fits perfectly in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Casual and personal writing
  • Journalism and reviews
  • Most non-academic contexts

In very formal or academic writing, some traditionalists prefer to avoid it and use constructions like "expressed enthusiasm" or "spoke enthusiastically" instead. This isn't because "enthuse" is wrong — it's a fully legitimate word — but because a small number of style guides still treat it with caution as a relatively modern coinage. In real-world usage, however, most writers and speakers use it freely and naturally.

PatternMeaningExample
  • "[Person] enthused about/over [thing]" → Person expressed enthusiasm about something

"She enthused about the film for hours."

  • "[Thing/Person] enthused [someone]" → Something made a person feel enthusiastic

"The workshop enthused all the participants."

  • "[Person] was/seemed enthused by/about [thing]" → Person felt enthusiastic (passive/adjective)

"He was enthused by the opportunity."
One Simple Way to Remember It

Think of enthuse as the doing word for enthusiasm.

Enthusiasm is the feeling. Enthusing is what you do when you have it — you show it, express it, radiate it. And sometimes, you pass it on to others.

That's the whole word.
